attributes.nuance_translation: An expression used to show a relatively low level of skill in something.

attributes.body:
～のが下手（へた） is a phrase that behaves in almost exactly the same way as ～のが上手（じょうず）, but rather than meaning 'to be good at (A)', it means 'to be bad at (A)', (which is a much more handy expression, if you are like me!). This particular expression is used with the plain (dictionary) form of verbs only.

In these examples, we can see that there is no difference between Ichidan verbs and Godan verbs. Both will appear in their plain form. In this expression, のが is performing the same function as in the regular のは, and のが constructions. This function is nominalization (turning a phrase into a noun).

Caution

If you want to express that you were bad at something (in the past), the verb will still remain in the plain form, but 下手（へた） will change to the past tense.

These phrases combine the nominalizer の with the な-Adjectives 好き and 下手. They are used to express liking something (好き) or not being good at something (下手). In Japanese culture, boasting is rare, so while 下手 can be used to humbly describe a lack of ability, 好き serves as a more modest alternative to the boastful-sounding 上手.

second_relatable.title: のがへた
second_relatable.meaning: To be bad at, Poor at, Unskillful

attributes.body: These two opposite terms are used after verbs to express being good or bad at certain actions. のが上手 is used to say someone is good at something, as in 絵を描くのが上手 ('She is good at drawing'). In contrast, 絵を描くのが下手 means 'She is not good at drawing.' Note that in Japanese culture, it's uncommon to use 上手 to describe yourself, as it can come across as boastful.
